'''''Melaleuca leucadendra''''', commonly known as '''weeping paperbark''', '''long-leaved paperbark''' or '''white paperbark''' is a species of woody plant in the [[Myrtus|myrtle]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Myrtaceae]], and is widespread in northern Australia, [[New Guinea]] and parts of [[Indonesia]]. It grows as a tree to more than {{convert|20|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} with a trunk covered with thick, white, papery bark and weeping thinner branches. It has a long flowering season, can flower at almost any time of the year and is often grown as a tree in parks and on roadsides. It was the first melaleuca to be described and was described from a specimen growing in Indonesia.

==Description==
''Melaleuca leucadendra'' is a large tree, usually less than, but sometimes more than {{convert|20|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall. Its thick bark is papery, usually white but also pinkish or cream and it has weeping branches. Its leaves and young branches are covered with fine, short, white hairs when young but become [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] as they mature. The leaves are arranged alternately, {{convert|75–270|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|6.5-40|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide, flat, narrow egg-shaped or lance-shaped and tapering to a point. The leaves have 5 (sometimes as many as 9) longitudinal veins and are often curved or sickle-shaped.<ref name="Brophy">{{cite book |last1=Brophy |first1=Joseph J. |last2=Craven |first2=Lyndley A. |last3=Doran |first3=John C. |title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses |date=2013 |publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research |location=Canberra |isbn=978-1-922137-51-7 |pages=224–225}}</ref><ref name="Holliday">{{cite book |last1=Holliday |first1=Ivan |title=Melaleucas : a field and garden guide |date=2004 |publisher=Reed New Holland Publishers |location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W. |isbn=1-876334-98-3 |pages=170–171 |edition=2nd}}</ref><ref name="JCU">{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca leucadendra''|url=https://www.jcu.edu.au/discover-nature-at-jcu/plants/plants-on-cairns-campus/melaleuca-leucadendra|publisher=James Cook University|accessdate=25 January 2018}}</ref>

The flowers are cream, white or greenish-white and are arranged in spikes on the ends of branches which continue to grow after flowering, sometimes on the sides of branches or in the upper leaf axils. Each spike is up to {{convert|35|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter, up to {{convert|80|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and contains between 7 and 22 groups of flowers in threes. The petals are {{convert|3-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide and fall off soon after the flower opens. The stamens are arranged in five bundles around the flower and each bundle contains 5 to 12 stamens. Flowering can occur at any time of the year and is followed by fruit which are woody [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]], {{convert|3.9-4.9|mm|in|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} long in loose clusters along the stems.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="Holliday" /><ref name="JCU" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Melaleuca leucadendra'' was first formally described in 1762 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in [[Species Plantarum]] as ''Myrtus leucadendra''.<ref name="Species">{{cite book|last1=Linnaeus|first1=Carl|title=Species Plantarum  |date=1762|volume=1 |page=676|edition=2|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/42877#page/692/mode/1up|accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref><ref name="APNI(1)">{{cite web|title=''Myrtus leucadendra''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/630984|publisher=APNI|accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref> Linnaeus used a description of the species written by [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius]] in 1741, before the modern system of classification was devised by Linnaeus. Rumphius had described a plant growing in what is now Indonesia. Later, Linnaeus realised that this species had little in common with other species in the [[genus]] ''[[Myrtus]]'' and described the genus ''[[Melaleuca]]'' to accommodate this species.<ref name="Brophy online">{{cite book |last1=Brophy |first1=Joseph J. |last2=Craven |first2=Lyndley A. |last3=Doran |first3=John C. |title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses |date=2013 |publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research |location=Canberra |isbn=978-1-922137-52-4 |page=15 |url=http://aciar.gov.au/files/mn156-prelims_1.pdf |accessdate=13 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528213958/http://aciar.gov.au/files/mn156-prelims_1.pdf |archive-date=28 May 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Thus, ''Melaleuca leucadendra'' became the first melaleuca to be formally described. The description was published in 1767 in ''Mantissa plantarum''.<ref name="Mantissa">{{cite book|last1=Linnaeus|first1=Carl|title=Mantissa plantarum|date=1767|page=105|url=http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/spa/Libro.php?Libro=947&Pagina=288|accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref><ref name="APNI(2)">{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca leucadendra''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/513481|publisher=APNI|accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref> It follows that although nearly all melaeucas are found only in Australia, the first [[Type (biology)|type specimen]] was from Indonesia.

The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''leucadendra'') is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] words ''[[wikt:λευκός|λευκός]] (leukós)'' meaning “white”<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.}}</ref>{{rp|856}} and ''[[wikt:δένδρον|δένδρον]] (déndron)'' meaning “tree”<ref name="RWB" />{{rp|813}} referring to the white bark of this plant.<ref name="Brophy" />

''Melaleuca leucadendra'' is superficially similar to other paperbark trees, especially ''[[Melaleuca cajuputi]]'', ''[[Melaleuca quinquenervia]]'', ''[[Melaleuca linariifolia]]'' and ''[[Melaleuca viridiflora]]'' and all are sometimes referred to as ''cajuput'' or ''cajeput''. ''[[wikt:cajuput|Cajuput]]'' is an [[English language|English]] word for [[Cajeput oil|the oil]] obtained from the foliage of ''Melaleuca cajuputi'' and the word is possibly a corruption of ''kayu putih'', the Indonesian name for the tree.<ref name="Brophy online(2)">{{cite book |last1=Brophy |first1=Joseph J. |last2=Craven |first2=Lyndley A. |last3=Doran |first3=John C. |title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses |date=2013 |publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research |location=Canberra |isbn=978-1-922137-52-4 |page=104 |url=http://aciar.gov.au/files/mn156-species-a-c_1.pdf |accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref> The [[Malay language|Malay]] name for the paperbark tree is ''gelam''<ref name="Wild">{{cite web|title=Gelam or Kayu putih|url=http://www.wildsingapore.com/wildfacts/plants/coastal/melaleuca/cajuputi.htm|publisher=Wild Singapore|accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref> and may have given its name to the [[Kampong Glam]] district in Singapore.<ref name="Keng">{{cite book |last1=Keng |first1=Hsuan |title=The Concise Flora of Singapore: Gymnosperms and dicotyledons |date=1990 |publisher=Singapore Univ. Press |location=Singapore |isbn=9971-69-135-3 |page=222}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This melaleuca is widely distributed in northern parts of [[Western Australia]], the [[Northern Territory]] and in [[Queensland]] as far south as [[Shoalwater Bay]]. It also occurs in [[New Guinea]] and  the [[Maluku Islands]] of Indonesia.<ref name="PoWO" /><ref name="Brophy" /> It grows in forests near the edges of rivers and streams on a range of soils.

==Uses==

===Traditional uses===
Aboriginal people used strips of bark from this tree and tied them to a frame of ''[[Dodonaea]]'' branches to build huts that were waterproof.  The bark was used to wrap food before cooking in an underground oven called a ''kap mari''. It was also used to wrap the bodies of their dead. The bark from trunks of very large trees was used to make bark canoes.<ref name="SGAP">{{cite web |last1=Calvert |first1=Greg |title=Bush tucker: White paperbark (''Melaleuca leucadendra'') |url=https://www.sgapqld.org.au/information-and-publications/bush-tucker-articles/254-white-paperbark|publisher=Society for growing Australian plants, Queensland |accessdate=25 January 2018}}</ref> The crushed leaves were used to treat respiratory infections and the flowers for making a sweet drink.<ref name="JCU" />

===Horticulture===
This species of melaleuca is often grown in parks and as a street tree in tropical and sub-tropical areas like [[Brisbane]]<ref name="Holliday" /> and as far south as [[Sydney]].<ref name="Wrigley">{{cite book |last1=Wrigley |first1=John W. |last2=Fagg |first2=Murray |title=Australian native plants : a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping |date=1983 |publisher=Collins |location=Sydney |isbn=0-00-216575-9 |pages=351–352 |edition=2nd}}</ref> It prefers a sunny location but will tolerate poor, waterlogged soils.<ref name="Waverley">{{cite web |title=''Melaleuca leucadendra'' |url=http://www.waverley.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/3000/Melaleuca_leucadendra.pdf |publisher=Waverley Council |accessdate=13 May 2015}}</ref> It has also been used as a street tree in Hong Kong.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jim |first1=C. Y. |year=1986 |title=Street trees in high-density urban Hong Kong |journal=Journal of Arboriculture |volume=12 |issue=10 |pages=257–263 |publisher=[[International Society of Arboriculture]] |url=http://joa.isa-arbor.com/request.asp?JournalID=1&ArticleID=2113&Type=2 |accessdate=12 August 2012}}</ref>

===Essential oils===
A range of essential oils can be distilled from this species, depending on where the trees occur. Two of the most common chemotypes are based on [[methyl eugenol]] and E-[[methyl isoeugenol]].<ref name="Brophy" />

===Timber===
The timber from ''M. leucadendra'' can be used for general construction. In Vietnam, it is used for poles, piles and woodchips.<ref name="Brophy" />
